119Whore, crocodile, that hast thy tears prepared,
120Expecting how thou'lt bid ‘em flow—

MOSCA

Expecting how thou'lt bid ‘em flow— Nay, pray you, sir!
121She will consider.

CELIA

She will consider. Would my life would serve
122To satisfy—

CORVINO

To satisfy— S'death! if she would but speak to him,
123And save my reputation, it were somewhat;
124But spitefully to affect my utter ruin!

MOSCA

125Aye, now you have put your fortune in her hands.
126Why i'faith, it is her modesty, I must quit her.
127If you were absent, she would be more coming;
128I know it: and dare undertake for her.
129What woman can before her husband? Pray you,
130Let us depart, and leave her here.

CORVINO

Let us depart, and leave her here. Sweet Celia,
131Thou may’st redeem all, yet; I'll say no more:
132If not, esteem yourself as lost.
If not, esteem yourself as lost. (Celia starts to leave.) Nay, stay there.

[Exeunt Corvino and Mosca.]

CELIA

133O God, and his good angels! whither, whither,
134Is shame fled human breasts? that with such ease,
135Men dare put off your honours, and their own?
136Is that, which ever was a cause of life,
137Now placed beneath the basest circumstance,
138And modesty an exile made, for money?

VOLPONE

139Aye, in Corvino, and such earth-fed minds,
140(He leaps off from his couch.) That never tasted the true heaven of love.
141Assure thee, Celia, he that would sell thee,
142Only for hope of gain, and that uncertain,
143He would have sold his part of Paradise
144For ready money, had he met a copeman.
145Why art thou mazed to see me thus revived?
146Rather applaud thy beauty's miracle;
147'Tis thy great work: that hath, not now alone,
148But sundry times raised me, in several shapes,
149And, but this morning, like a mountebank,
150To see thee at thy window: aye, before
151I would have left my practice, for thy love,
152In varying figures, I would have contended
153With the blue Proteus, or the horned flood.
154Now art thou welcome.

CELIA

Now art thou welcome. Sir!

VOLPONE

Now art thou welcome. Sir! Nay, fly me not.
155Nor let thy false imagination
156That I was bed-rid, make thee think I am so:
157Thou shalt not find it. I am, now, as fresh,
158As hot, as high, and in as jovial plight,
159As when, in that so celebrated scene,
160At recitation of our comedy,
161For entertainment of the great Valois,
162I acted young Antinous, and attracted
163The eyes and ears of all the ladies present,
164To admire each graceful gesture, note, and footing.

(Song.)

165Come, my Celia, let us prove,
166While we can, the sports of love,
167Time will not be ours for ever,
168He, at length, our good will sever;
169Spend not then his gifts in vain;
170Suns, that set, may rise again;
171But if once we lose this light,
172'Tis with us perpetual night.
173Why should we defer our joys?
174Fame and rumour are but toys.
175Cannot we delude the eyes
176Of a few poor household spies?
177Or his easier ears beguile,
178Thus removed by our wile?—
179'Tis no sin love's fruits to steal:
180But the sweet thefts to reveal;
181To be taken, to be seen,
182These have crimes accounted been.

CELIA

183Some serene blast me, or dire lightning strike
184This my offending face!

VOLPONE

This my offending face! Why droops my Celia?
185Thou hast, in place of a base husband, found
186A worthy lover: use thy fortune well,
187With secrecy and pleasure. See, behold,
188What thou art queen of; not in expectation,
189As I feed others: but possessed and crowned.
190See, here, a rope of pearl; and each, more orient
191Than that the brave Egyptian queen caroused;
192Dissolve and drink them. See, a carbuncle,
193May put out both the eyes of our St. Mark;
194A diamond, would have bought Lollia Paulina,
195When she came in like star-light, hid with jewels,
196That were the spoils of provinces; take these,
197And wear, and lose them: yet remains an ear-ring
198To purchase them again, and this whole state.
199A gem but worth a private patrimony,
200Is nothing: we will eat such at a meal.
201The heads of parrots, tongues of nightingales,
202The brains of peacocks, and of ostriches,
203Shall be our food: and, could we get the phoenix,
204Though nature lost her kind, she were our dish.

CELIA

205Good sir, these things might move a mind affected
206With such delights; but I, whose innocence
207Is all I can think wealthy, or worth the enjoying,
208And which, once lost, I have naught to lose beyond it,
209Cannot be taken with these sensual baits:
210If you have conscience—

VOLPONE

If you have conscience— 'Tis the beggar's virtue;
211If thou hast wisdom, hear me, Celia.
212Thy baths shall be the juice of July-flowers,
213Spirit of roses, and of violets,
214The milk of unicorns, and panthers' breath
215Gathered in bags, and mixed with Cretan wines.
216Our drink shall be prepared gold and amber,
217Which we will take, until my roof whirl round
218With the vertigo: and my dwarf shall dance,
219My eunuch sing, my fool make up the antic,
220Whilst we, in changed shapes, act Ovid's tales,
221Thou, like Europa now, and I like Jove,
222Then I like Mars, and thou like Erycine:
223So, of the rest, till we have quite run through,
224And wearied all the fables of the gods.
225Then will I have thee in more modern forms,
226Attired like some sprightly dame of France,
227Brave Tuscan lady, or proud Spanish beauty;
228Sometimes, unto the Persian Sophy's wife;
229Or the Grand Signior's mistress; and, for change,
230To one of our most artful courtesans,
231Or some quick Negro, or cold Russian;
232And I will meet thee in as many shapes:
233Where we may so transfuse our wandering souls
234Out at our lips, and score up sums of pleasures,
235[Sings.] That the curious shall not know
236How to tell them as they flow;
237And the envious, when they find
238What their number is, be pined.

CELIA

239If you have ears that will be pierced—or eyes
240That can be opened—a heart that may be touched—
241Or any part that yet sounds man about you—
242If you have touch of holy saints—or heaven—
243Do me the grace to let me ‘scape—if not,
244Be bountiful and kill me. You do know,
245I am a creature, hither ill betrayed,
246By one, whose shame I would forget it were.—
247If you will deign me neither of these graces,
248Yet feed your wrath, sir, rather than your lust —
249(It is a vice comes nearer manliness)—
250And punish that unhappy crime of nature,
251Which you miscall my beauty— flay my face,
252Or poison it with ointments, for seducing
253Your blood to this rebellion—Rub these hands,
254With what may cause an eating leprosy,
255E'en to my bones and marrow— any thing,
256That may disfavour me, save in my honour—
257And I will kneel to you, pray for you, pay down
258A thousand hourly vows, sir, for your health
259Report and think you virtuous—

VOLPONE

Report and think you virtuous— Think me cold,
260Frozen and impotent, and so report me?
261That I had Nestor's hernia, thou wouldst think.
262I do degenerate, and abuse my nation,
263To play with opportunity thus long;
264I should have done the act, and then have parleyed.
265Yield, or I'll force thee.

CELIA

Yield, or I'll force thee. O! just God!

VOLPONE

Yield, or I'll force thee. O! just God! In vain –

BONARIO

266(He leaps out from where Mosca had placed him.) Forbear, foul ravisher, libidinous swine!
267Free the forced lady, or thou diest, impostor.
268But that I'm loath to snatch thy punishment
269Out of the hand of justice, thou shouldst, yet,
270Be made the timely sacrifice of vengeance,
271Before this altar, and this dross, thy idol.—
272Lady, let's quit the place., it is the den
273Of villainy; fear naught, you have a guard:
274And he, ere long, shall meet his just reward.

[Exeunt Bonario and Celia.]

VOLPONE

275Fall on me, roof, and bury me in ruin!
276Become my grave, that wert my shelter! O!
277I am unmasked, unspirited, undone,
278Betrayed to beggary, to infamy—

ACT 3, SCENE 8

[Enter Mosca, bleeding.]

MOSCA

1Where shall I run, most wretched shame of men,
2To beat out my unlucky brains?

VOLPONE

To beat out my unlucky brains? Here, here.
3What! dost thou bleed?

MOSCA

What! dost thou bleed? O that his well-driven sword
4Had been so courteous to have cleft me down
5Unto the navel, ere I lived to see
6My life, my hopes, my spirits, my patron, all
7Thus desperately engaged, by my error!

VOLPONE

8Woe on thy fortune!

MOSCA

Woe on thy fortune! And my follies, sir.

VOLPONE

9Thou hast made me miserable.

MOSCA

Thou hast made me miserable. And myself, sir.
10Who would have thought he would have hearkened so?

VOLPONE

11What shall we do?

MOSCA

What shall we do? I know not; if my heart
12Could expiate the mischance, I'd pluck it out.
13Will you be pleased to hang me, or cut my throat?
14And I'll requite you, sir. Let's die like Romans,
15Since we have lived like Grecians.

[They knock without.]

VOLPONE

Since we have lived like Grecians. Hark! who's there?
16I hear some footing: officers, the Saffi,
17Come to apprehend us! I do feel the brand
18Hissing already at my forehead; now
19Mine ears are boring.

MOSCA

Mine ears are boring. To your couch, sir, you
20[Volpone lies down.]{tf}Guilty men Make that place good, however.
21Suspect what they deserve still.
Suspect what they deserve still. [Opens door.] Signior Corbaccio!

ACT 3, SCENE 9

[Enter Corbaccio .]

CORBACCIO

1Why, how now, Mosca!

[Enter Voltore, behind]

MOSCA

Why, how now, Mosca! Oh, undone, amazed, sir.
2Your son, I know not by what accident,
3Acquainted with your purpose to my patron,
4Touching your will, and making him your heir,
5Entered our house with violence, his sword drawn,
6Sought for you, called you wretch, unnatural,
7Vowed he would kill you.

CORBACCIO

Vowed he would kill you. Me!

MOSCA

Vowed he would kill you. Me! Yes, and my patron.

CORBACCIO

8This act shall disinherit him indeed;
9Here is the will.

MOSCA

Here is the will. 'Tis well, sir.

CORBACCIO

Here is the will. 'Tis well, sir. Right and well:
10Be you as careful now for me.

MOSCA

Be you as careful now for me. My life, sir,
11Is not more tendered; I am only yours.

CORBACCIO

12How does he? Will he die shortly,
13think'st thou?

MOSCA

think'st thou? I fear
14He'll outlast May.

CORBACCIO

He'll outlast May. To-day?

MOSCA

He'll outlast May. To-day? No, last our May, sir.

CORBACCIO

15Could’st thou not give him a dram?

MOSCA

Could’st thou not give him a dram? O, by no means, sir.

CORBACCIO

16Nay, I'll not bid you.

VOLTORE

Nay, I'll not bid you. [Aside.] This is a knave, I see.aparte

MOSCA

17[Aside.] How! Signior Voltore! Did he hear me?aparte

VOLTORE

[Aside.] How! Signior Voltore! Did he hear me? Parasite!

MOSCA

18Who's that? O, sir, most timely welcome—

[joins Voltore]

VOLTORE

Who's that? O, sir, most timely welcome— Scarce,
19To the discovery of your tricks, I fear.
20You are his, only? And mine also, are you not?

MOSCA

21Who? I, sir?

VOLTORE

Who? I, sir? You, sir. What device is this
22About a will?

MOSCA

About a will? A plot for you, sir.

VOLTORE

About a will? A plot for you, sir. Come,
23Put not your foists upon me; I shall scent them.

MOSCA

24Did you not hear it?

VOLTORE

Did you not hear it? Yes, I hear Corbaccio
25Hath made your patron there his heir.

MOSCA

Hath made your patron there his heir. 'Tis true,
26By my device, drawn to it by my plot,
27With hope—

VOLTORE

With hope— Your patron should reciprocate?
28And you have promised?

MOSCA

And you have promised? For your good I did, sir.
29Nay, more, I told his son, brought, hid him here,
30Where he might hear his father pass the deed:
31Being persuaded to it by this thought, sir,
32That the unnaturalness, first, of the act,
33And then his father's oft disclaiming in him
34(Which I did mean t' help on) would sure enrage him
35To do some violence upon his parent,
36On which the law should take sufficient hold,
37And you be stated in a double hope:
38Truth be my comfort, and my conscience,
39My only aim was to dig you a fortune
40Out of these two old rotten sepulchres –

VOLTORE

41I cry thee mercy, Mosca.

MOSCA

I cry thee mercy, Mosca. Worth your patience,
42And your great merit, sir. And see the change!

VOLTORE

43Why, what success?

MOSCA

Why, what success? Most hapless! You must help, sir.
44Whilst we expected the old raven, in comes
45Corvino's wife, sent hither by her husband –

VOLTORE

46What, with a present?

MOSCA

What, with a present? No, sir, on visitation –
47I'll tell you how anon — and staying long,
48The youth he grows impatient, rushes forth,
49Seizeth the lady, wounds me, makes her swear –
50Or he would murder her, that was his vow –
51To affirm my patron to have done her rape,
52Which how unlike it is, you see! and hence,
53With that pretext he's gone, to accuse his father,
54Defame my patron, defeat you –

VOLTORE

Defame my patron, defeat you – Where is her husband?
55Let him be sent for straight.

MOSCA

Let him be sent for straight. Sir, I'll go fetch him.

VOLTORE

56Bring him to the Scrutineo.

MOSCA

Bring him to the Scrutineo. Sir, I will.

VOLTORE

57This must be stopped.

MOSCA

This must be stopped. O you do nobly, sir.
58Alas, 'twas laboured all, sir, for your good;
59Nor was there want of counsel in the plot:
60But fortune can, at any time, o’erthrow
61The projects of a hundred learned clerks, sir.

CORBACCIO

62[Listening] What's that?

VOLTORE

[Listening] What's that? Will't please you, sir, to go along?

[Exeunt Corbaccio and Voltore.]

MOSCA

63Patron, go in, and pray for our success.

VOLTORE

64Need makes devotion: heaven your labour bless!

[Exeunt]

ACT 4

SCENE 1

[Enter Sir Politic Would-be and Peregrine.]

SIR POLITIC

1I told you, sir, it was a plot: you see
2What observation is! You mentioned me
3For some instructions: I will tell you, sir
4(Since we are met here in the height of Venice),
5Some few particulars I have set down,
6Only for this meridian, fit to be known
7Of your crude traveller, and they are these.
8I will not touch, sir, at your phrase, or clothes,
9For they are old.

PEREGRINE

For they are old. Sir, I have better.

SIR POLITIC

For they are old. Sir, I have better. Pardon,
10I meant as they are themes.

PEREGRINE

I meant as they are themes. O, sir, proceed:
11I'll slander you no more of wit, good sir.

SIR POLITIC

12First, for your garb, it must be grave and serious,
13Very reserved and locked; not tell a secret
14On any terms, not to your father, scarce
15A fable, but with caution: make sure choice
16Both of your company, and discourse; beware
17You never speak a truth –

PEREGRINE

You never speak a truth – How!

SIR POLITIC

You never speak a truth – How! Not to strangers,
18For those be they you must converse with most;
19Others I would not know, sir, but at distance,
20So as I still might be a saver in them:
21You shall have tricks else past upon you hourly.
22And then, for your religion, profess none,
23But wonder at the diversity of all:
24And, for your part, protest, were there no other
25But simply the laws o' the land, you could content you,
26Nick Machiavel, and Monsieur Bodin, both
27Were of this mind. Then must you learn the use
28And handling of your silver fork at meals,
29The metal of your glass; (these are main matters
30With your Italian;) and to know the hour
31When you must eat your melons, and your figs.

PEREGRINE

32Is that a point of state, too?

SIR POLITIC

Is that a point of state, too? Here it is:
33For your Venetian, if he see a man
34Preposterous in the least, he has him straight;
35He has: he strips him. I'll acquaint you, sir.
36I now have lived here, 'tis some fourteen months;
37Within the first week of my landing here,
38All took me for a citizen of Venice,
39I knew the forms so well –

PEREGRINE

I knew the forms so well – [Aside.] And nothing else.aparte

SIR POLITIC

40I had read Contarine, took me a house,
41Dealt with my Jews to furnish it with moveables –
42Well, if I could but find one man, one man
43To mine own heart, whom I durst trust, I would –

PEREGRINE

44What, what, sir?

SIR POLITIC

What, what, sir? Make him rich; make him a fortune:
45He should not think again. I would command it.

PEREGRINE

46As how?

SIR POLITIC

As how? With certain projects that I have –
47Which I may not discover.

PEREGRINE

Which I may not discover. [Aside.] If I hadaparte
48But one to wager with, I would lay odds now,
49He tells me instantly.

SIR POLITIC

He tells me instantly. One is, and that
50I care not greatly who knows, to serve the state
51Of Venice with red herrings for three years,
52And at a certain rate, from Rotterdam,
53Where I have correspondence. There's a letter,
54Sent me from one o' the States, and to that purpose:
55He cannot write his name, but that's his mark.

PEREGRINE

56He is a chandler?

SIR POLITIC

He is a chandler? No, a cheesemonger.
57There are some others too, with whom I treat
58About the same negotiation;
59And I will undertake it: for 'tis thus.
60I'll do't with ease, I have cast it all: Your hoy
61Carries but three men in her and a boy;
62And she shall make me three returns a year:
63So, if there come but one of three, I save;
64If two, I can defalk. But this is now,
65If my main project fail.

PEREGRINE

If my main project fail. Then you have others?

SIR POLITIC

66I should be loath to draw the subtle air
67Of such a place, without my thousand aims.
68I'll not dissemble, sir: where'er I come,
69I love to be considerative; and 'tis true,
70I have at my free hours thought upon
71Some certain goods unto the state of Venice,
72Which I do call my cautions; and, sir, which
73I mean, in hope of pension, to propound
74To the Great Council, then unto the Forty,
75So to the Ten. My means are made already –

PEREGRINE

76By whom?

SIR POLITIC

By whom? Sir, one that though his place be obscure,
77Yet he can sway, and they will hear him. He's
78A commendatore.

PEREGRINE

A commendatore. What, a common sergeant?

SIR POLITIC

79Sir, such as they are, put it in their mouths,
80What they should say, sometimes; as well as greater:
81I think I have my notes to show you –

PEREGRINE

I think I have my notes to show you – Good sir.

SIR POLITIC

82But you shall swear unto me, on your gentry,
83Not to anticipate –

PEREGRINE

Not to anticipate – I, sir!

SIR POLITIC

Not to anticipate – I, sir! Nor reveal
84A circumstance – My paper is not with me.

PEREGRINE

85O, but you can remember, sir.

SIR POLITIC

O, but you can remember, sir. My first is
86Concerning tinder-boxes. You must know
87No family is here without its box.
88Now, sir, it being so portable a thing,
89Put case, that you or I were ill affected
90Unto the state, sir; with it in our pockets
91Might not I go into the Arsenale,
92Or you, come out again, and none the wiser?

PEREGRINE

93Except yourself, sir.

SIR POLITIC

Except yourself, sir. Go to, then. I therefore
94Advertise to the state, how fit it were,
95That none but such as were known patriots,
96Sound lovers of their country, should be suffered
97To enjoy them in their houses; and even those
98Sealed at some office, and at such a bigness
99As might not lurk in pockets.

PEREGRINE

As might not lurk in pockets. Admirable!

SIR POLITIC

100My next is, how to inquire, and be resolved,
101By present demonstration, whether a ship,
102Newly arrived from Soria, or from
103Any suspected part of all the Levant,
104Be guilty of the plague: and where they use
105To lie out forty, fifty days, sometimes
106About the Lazaretto, for their trial;
107I'll save that charge and loss unto the merchant,
108And in an hour clear the doubt.

PEREGRINE

And in an hour clear the doubt. Indeed, sir!

SIR POLITIC

109Or – I will lose my labour.

PEREGRINE

Or – I will lose my labour. My faith, that's much.

SIR POLITIC

110Nay, sir, conceive me. It will cost me in onions,
111Some thirty livres –

PEREGRINE

Some thirty livres – Which is one pound sterling.

SIR POLITIC

112Beside my water-works: for this I do, sir,
113First, I bring in your ship 'twixt two brick walls;
114But those the state shall venture: on the one
115I strain me a fair tarpaulin, and in that
116I stick my onions, cut in halves: the other
117Is full of loop-holes, out at which I thrust
118The noses of my bellows; and those bellows
119I keep, with water-works, in perpetual motion,
120Which is the easiest matter of a hundred.
121Now, sir, your onion, which doth naturally
122Attract the infection, and your bellows blowing
123The air upon him, will show, instantly,
124By his changed colour, if there be contagion;
125Or else remain as fair as at the first.
126—Now it is known, 'tis nothing.

PEREGRINE

—Now it is known, 'tis nothing. You are right, sir.

SIR POLITIC

127I would I had my note.

PEREGRINE

I would I had my note. Faith, so would I:
128But you have done well for once, sir.

SIR POLITIC

But you have done well for once, sir. Were I false,
129Or would be made so, I could show you reasons
130How I could sell this state now to the Turk,
131Spite of their galleys, or their –

PEREGRINE

Spite of their galleys, or their – Pray you, sir Politic.

SIR POLITIC

132I have them not about me.

PEREGRINE

I have them not about me. That I feared:
133They are there, sir.

SIR POLITIC

They are there, sir. No, this is my diary,
134Wherein I note my actions of the day.

PEREGRINE

135Pray you, let's see, sir. What is here?
136“Notandum,
137A rat had gnawn my spur leathers; notwithstanding,
138I put on new, and did go forth: but first
139I threw three beans over the threshold. Item,
140I went and bought two toothpicks, whereof one
141I burst immediately, in a discourse
142With a Dutch merchant, 'bout ragion’ del stato.
143From him I went and paid a mocenigo
144For piecing my silk stockings; by the way
145I cheapened sprats; and at St. Mark's I urined.
146Faith, these are politic notes!

SIR POLITIC

Faith, these are politic notes! Sir, I do slip
147No action of my life, but thus I quote it.

PEREGRINE

148Believe me, it is wise!

SIR POLITIC

Believe me, it is wise! Nay, sir, read forth.

ACT 4, SCENE 2

(Enter Lady Politic Would-be, Nano, and the two Women.)

LADY POLITIC

1Where should this loose knight be, trow?
2Sure he's housed.

NANO

Sure he's housed. Why, then he's fast.

LADY POLITIC

3Aye, he plays both with me.
4I pray you stay. This heat will do more harm
5To my complexion, than his heart is worth.
6I do not care to hinder, but to take him.—
7How it comes off!
How it comes off! My master's yonder.

LADY POLITIC

How it comes off! My master's yonder. Where?
8With a young gentleman.

LADY POLITIC

With a young gentleman. That same's the party;
9In man's apparel! Pray you, sir, jog my knight:
10I will be tender to his reputation,
11However he demerit.

SIR POLITIC

However he demerit. My lady!

PEREGRINE

However he demerit. My lady! Where?

SIR POLITIC

12'Tis she indeed, sir; you shall know her. She is,
13Were she not mine, a lady of that merit,
14For fashion and behaviour; and for beauty
15I durst compare –

PEREGRINE

I durst compare – It seems you are not jealous,
16That dare commend her.

SIR POLITIC

That dare commend her. Nay, and for discourse –

PEREGRINE

17Being your wife, she cannot miss that.

SIR POLITIC

Being your wife, she cannot miss that. Madam,
18Here is a gentleman; pray you use him fairly;
19He seems a youth, but he is—

LADY POLITIC

He seems a youth, but he is— None.

SIR POLITIC

He seems a youth, but he is— None. Yes, one
20Has put his face as soon into the world –

LADY POLITIC

21You mean, as early? But to-day?

SIR POLITIC

You mean, as early? But to-day? How's this?

LADY POLITIC

22Why, in this habit, sir; you apprehend me:—
23Well, Master Would-be, this doth not become you;
24I had thought the odour, sir, of your good name
25Had been more precious to you; that you would not
26Have done this dire massacre on your honour;
27One of your gravity and rank besides!
28But knights, I see, care little for the oath
29They make to ladies; chiefly, their own ladies.

SIR POLITIC

30Now, by my spurs, the symbol of my knighthood, –

PEREGRINE

31(Aside.) Lord, how his brain is humbled for an oath!aparte

SIR POLITIC

32I reach you not.

LADY POLITIC

I reach you not. Right, sir, your policy
33May bear it through thus.
May bear it through thus. [To Peregrine] —Sir, a word with you.
34I would be loath to contest publicly
35With any gentlewoman, or to seem
36Forward, or violent; as The Courtier says;
37It comes too near rusticity in a lady,
38Which I would shun by all means: and however
39I may deserve from master Would-be, yet
40T' have one fair gentlewoman thus be made
41The unkind instrument to wrong another,
42And one she knows not, aye, and to perséver;
43In my poor judgment, is not warranted
44From being a solecism in our sex,
45If not in manners.

PEREGRINE

If not in manners. How is this!

SIR POLITIC

If not in manners. How is this! Sweet madam,
46Come nearer to your aim.

LADY POLITIC

Come nearer to your aim. Marry, and will, sir.
47Since you provoke me with your impudence,
48And laughter of your light land-siren here,
49Your Sporus, your hermaphrodite—.

PEREGRINE

Your Sporus, your hermaphrodite—. What's here?
50Poetic fury and historic storms!

SIR POLITIC

51The gentleman, believe it, is of worth,
52And of our nation.

LADY POLITIC

And of our nation. Aye, your Whitefriars nation.
53Come, I blush for you, Master Would-be, I:
54And am ashamed you should have no more forehead,
55Than thus to be the patron, or St. George,
56To a lewd harlot, a base fricatrice,
57A female devil, in a male outside.

SIR POLITIC

A female devil, in a male outside. Nay,
58An you be such a one, I must bid adieu
59To your delights. The case appears too liquid.

[Exit.]

LADY POLITIC

60Aye, you may carry't clear, with your state-face!—
61But for your carnival concupiscence,
62Who here is fled for liberty of conscience,
63From furious persecution of the marshal,
64Her will I disple.

PEREGRINE

Her will I disple. This is fine, i'faith!
65And do you use this often? Is this part
66Of your wit's exercise, 'gainst you have occasion?
67Madam –

LADY POLITIC

Madam – Go to, sir.

PEREGRINE

Madam – Go to, sir. Do you hear me, lady?
68Why, if your knight have set you to beg shirts,
69Or to invite me home, you might have done it
70A nearer way, by far.

LADY POLITIC

A nearer way, by far. This cannot work you
71Out of my snare.

PEREGRINE

Out of my snare. Why, am I in it, then?
72Indeed your husband told me you were fair.
73And so you are; only your nose inclines,
74That side that's next the sun, to the queen-apple.

LADY POLITIC

75This cannot be endured by any patience.

ACT 4, SCENE 3

[Enter Mosca]

MOSCA

1What is the matter, madam?

LADY POLITIC

What is the matter, madam? If the Senate
2Right not my quest in this, I will protest them
3To all the world, no aristocracy.

MOSCA

To all the world, no aristocracy. What is the injury, lady?

LADY POLITIC

To all the world, no aristocracy. What is the injury, lady? Why, the callet
4You told me of, here I have ta’en disguised.

MOSCA

5Who? this! What means your ladyship? The creature
6I mentioned to you is apprehended now,
7Before the senate; you shall see her –

LADY POLITIC

Before the senate; you shall see her – Where?

MOSCA

8I'll bring you to her. This young gentlernan,
9I saw him land this morning at the port.

LADY POLITIC

10Is't possible? How has my judgment wandered?
11Sir, I must, blushing, say to you, I have erred;
12And plead your pardon.

PEREGRINE

And plead your pardon. What, more changes yet?

LADY POLITIC

13I hope you have not the malice to remember
14A gentlewoman's passion. If you stay
15In Venice here, please you to use me, sir —

MOSCA

16Will you go, madam?

LADY POLITIC

Will you go, madam? Pray you, sir, use me; in faith,
17The more you see me, the more I shall conceive
18You have forgot our quarrel.

[Exeunt Mosca, Lady Would-be, Nano, and Waiting- women.]

PEREGRINE

You have forgot our quarrel. This is rare!
19Sir Politick Would-be? No; Sir Politick Bawd,
20To bring me thus acquainted with his wife!
21Well, wise Sir Pol, since you have practised thus
22Upon my freshmanship, I'll try your salt-head,
23What proof it is against a counter-plot.

ACT 4, SCENE 4

[Enter Voltore, Corbaccio, Corvino, and Mosca.]

VOLTORE

1Well, now you know the carriage of the business,
2Your constancy is all that is required
3Unto the safety of it.

MOSCA

Unto the safety of it. Is the lie
4Safely conveyed amongst us? is that sure?
5Knows every man his burden?

CORVINO

Knows every man his burden? Yes.

MOSCA

Knows every man his burden? Yes. Then shrink not.

CORVINO

6But knows the advocate the truth?

MOSCA

But knows the advocate the truth? O, sir,
7By no means; I devised a formal tale,
8That salved your reputation. But be valiant, sir.

CORVINO

9I fear no one but him, that this his pleading
10Should make him stand for a co-heir—

MOSCA

Should make him stand for a co-heir— Co-halter!
11Hang him; we will but use his tongue, his noise,
12As we do Croaker’s, here.

CORVINO

As we do Croaker’s, here. Aye, what shall he do?

MOSCA

13When we have done, you mean?

CORVINO

When we have done, you mean? Yes.

MOSCA

When we have done, you mean? Yes. Why, we'll think –
14Sell him for mummia; he's half dust already.
15(To Voltore.) Do you not smile, to see this buffalo,
16How he doth sport it with his head?
How he doth sport it with his head? [Aside.] I should,aparte
17If all were well and past.
If all were well and past. (To Corbaccio) Sir, only you
18Are he that shall enjoy the crop of all,
19And these not know for whom they toil.

CORBACCIO

And these not know for whom they toil. Aye, peace.

MOSCA

20(To Corvino) But you shall eat it. Much!
(To Corvino) But you shall eat it. Much! (Then to Voltore again) —Worshipful sir,
21Mercury sit upon your thundering tongue,
22Or the French Hercules, and make your language
23As conquering as his club, to beat along,
24As with a tempest, flat, our adversaries;
25But much more yours, sir.

VOLTORE

But much more yours, sir. Here they come, have done.

MOSCA

26I have another witness, if you need, sir,
27I can produce.

VOLTORE

I can produce. Who is it?

MOSCA

I can produce. Who is it? Sir, I have her.

ACT 4, SCENE 5

(Enter 4 Avocatori, Bonario, Celia, Notario, Commendatori, and Others.)

1 AVOCATORI

1The like of this the Senate never heard of.

2 AVOCATORI

2'Twill come most strange to them when we report it.

4 AVOCATORI

3The gentlewoman has been ever held
4Of unreproved name.

3 AVOCATORI

Of unreproved name. So, the young man.

4 AVOCATORI

5The more unnatural part that of his father.

2 AVOCATORI

6More of the husband.

1 AVOCATORI

More of the husband. I not know to give
7His act a name, it is so monstrous!

4 AVOCATORI

8But the impostor, he's a thing created
9To exceed example!

1 AVOCATORI

To exceed example! And all after-times!

2 AVOCATORI

10I never heard a true voluptuary
11Described, but him.

3 AVOCATORI

Described, but him. Appear yet those were cited?

NOTARIO

12All but the old magnifico, Volpone.

1 AVOCATORI

13Why is not he here?

MOSCA

14Please your fatherhoods,
15Here is his advocate: himself's so weak,
16So feeble –

4 AVOCATORI

So feeble – What are you?

BONARIO

So feeble – What are you? His parasite,
17His knave, his pander. I beseech the court
18He may be forced to come, that your grave eyes
19May bear strong witness of his strange impostures.

VOLTORE

20Upon my faith and credit with your virtues,
21He is not able to endure the air.

2 AVOCATORI

22Bring him, however.

3 AVOCATORI

Bring him, however. We will see him.

4 AVOCATORI

Bring him, however. We will see him. Fetch him.

VOLTORE

23Your fatherhoods' fit pleasures be obeyed;
24But sure, the sight will rather move your pities,
25Than indignation. May it please the court,
26In the mean time, he may be heard in me;
27I know this place most void of prejudice,
28And therefore crave it, since we have no reason
29To fear our truth should hurt our cause.

3 AVOCATORI

To fear our truth should hurt our cause. Speak free.

VOLTORE

30Then know, most honoured fathers, I must now
31Discover to your strangely abusèd ears,
32The most prodigious and most frontless piece
33Of solid impudence, and treachery,
34That ever vicious nature yet brought forth
35To shame the state of Venice. This lewd woman,
36That wants no artificial looks or tears
37To help the visor she has now put on,
38Hath long been known a close adulteress
39To that lascivious youth there; not suspected,
40I say, but known, and taken in the act
41With him; and by this man, the easy husband,
42Pardoned; whose timeless bounty makes him now
43Stand here, the most unhappy, innocent person,
44That ever man's own goodness made accused.
45For these not knowing how to owe a gift
46Of that dear grace, but with their shame; being placed
47So above all powers of their gratitude,
48Began to hate the benefit; and, in place
49Of thanks, devise to extirpe the memory
50Of such an act: wherein I pray your fatherhoods
51To observe the malice, yea, the rage of creatures
52Discovered in their evils; and what heart
53Such take, even from their crimes:— but that anon
54Will more appear.—This gentleman, the father,
55Hearing of this foul fact, with many others,
56Which daily struck at his too tender ears,
57And grieved in nothing more than that he could not
58Preserve himself a parent, (his son's ills
59Growing to that strange flood,) at last decreed
60To disinherit him.

1 AVOCATORI

To disinherit him. These be strange turns!

2 AVOCATORI

61The young man's fame was ever fair and honest.

VOLTORE

62So much more full of danger is his vice,
63That can beguile so under shade of virtue.
64But, as I said, my honoured sires, his father
65Having this settled purpose, by what means
66To him betrayed, we know not, and this day
67Appointed for the deed; that parricide,
68I cannot style him better, by confederacy
69Preparing this his paramour to be there,
70Entered Volpone's house, (who was the man,
71Your fatherhoods must understand, designed
72For the inheritance,) there sought his father:—
73But with what purpose sought he him, my lords?
74(I tremble to pronounce it, that a son
75Unto a father, and to such a father,
76Should have so foul, felonious intent)
77It was to murder him. When, being prevented
78By his more happy absence, what then did he?
79Not check his wicked thoughts: no, now new deeds:
80(Mischief doth never end where it begins)
81An act of horror, fathers! he dragged forth
82The agèd gentleman that had there lain bed-rid
83Three years and more, out of his innocent couch,
84Naked upon the floor, there left him; wounded
85His servant in the face: and with this strumpet
86The stale to his forged practice, who was glad
87To be so active, (I shall here desire
88Your Fatherhoods to note but my collections,
89As most remarkable) thought, at once, to stop
90His father's ends; discredit his free choice,
91In the old gentleman; redeem themselves,
92By laying infamy upon this man,
93To whom, with blushing, they should owe their lives.

1 AVOCATORI

94What proofs have you of this?

BONARIO

What proofs have you of this? Most honored fathers,
95I humbly crave there be no credit given
96To this man's mercenary tongue.

2 AVOCATORI

To this man's mercenary tongue. Forbear.

BONARIO

97His soul moves in his fee.

3 AVOCATORI

His soul moves in his fee. O, sir.

BONARIO

His soul moves in his fee. O, sir. This fellow,
98For six sols more, would plead against his maker.

1 AVOCATORI

99You do forget yourself.

VOLTORE

You do forget yourself. Nay, nay, grave fathers,
100Let him have scope: can any man imagine
101That he will spare his accuser, that would not
102Have spared his parent?

1 AVOCATORI

Have spared his parent? Well, produce your proofs.

CELIA

103I would I could forget I were a creature.

VOLTORE

104Signior Corbaccio!

4 AVOCATORI

Signior Corbaccio! What is he?

VOLTORE

Signior Corbaccio! What is he? The father.

2 AVOCATORI

105Has he had an oath?

NOTARIO

Has he had an oath? Yes.

CORBACCIO

Has he had an oath? Yes. What must I do now?

NOTARIO

106Your testimony's craved.

CORBACCIO

Your testimony's craved. Speak to the knave?
107I'll have my mouth first stopped with earth; my heart
108Abhors his knowledge: I disclaim in him.

1 AVOCATORI

109But for what cause?

CORBACCIO

But for what cause? The mere portent of nature!
110He is an utter stranger to my loins.

BONARIO

111Have they made you to this?

CORBACCIO

Have they made you to this? I will not hear thee,
112Monster of men, swine, goat, wolf, parricide!
113Speak not, thou viper.

BONARIO

Speak not, thou viper. Sir, I will sit down,
114And rather wish my innocence should suffer,
115Than I resist the authority of a father.

VOLTORE

116Signior Corvino!

2 AVOCATORI

Signior Corvino! This is strange.

1 AVOCATORI

Signior Corvino! This is strange. Who's this?

NOTARIO

117The husband.

4 AVOCATORI

The husband. Is he sworn?

NOTARIO

The husband. Is he sworn? He is.

3 AVOCATORI

The husband. Is he sworn? He is. Speak, then.

CORVINO

118This woman, please your fatherhoods, is a whore,
119Of most hot exercise, more than a partridge,
120Upon record –

1 AVOCATORI

Upon record – No more.

CORVINO

Upon record – No more. Neighs like a jennet.

NOTARIO

121Preserve the honour of the court.

CORVINO

Preserve the honour of the court. I shall,
122And modesty of your most reverend ears.
123And yet I hope that I may say, these eyes
124Have seen her glued unto that piece of cedar,
125That fine well-timbered gallant; and that here
126The letters may be read, thorough the horn,
127That makes the story perfect.

MOSCA

That makes the story perfect. Excellent! sir.

CORVINO

128There is no shame in this now, is there?

MOSCA

There is no shame in this now, is there? None.

CORVINO

129Or if I said, I hoped that she were onward
130To her damnation, if there be a hell
131Greater than whore and woman; a good Christian
132May make the doubt.

3 AVOCATORI

May make the doubt. His grief hath made him frantic.

1 AVOCATORI

133Remove him hence.

2 AVOCATORI

Remove him hence. Look to the woman.

CORVINO

Remove him hence. Look to the woman. Rare!
134Prettily feigned, again!

4 AVOCATORI

Prettily feigned, again! Stand from about her.

1 AVOCATORI

135Give her the air.

3 AVOCATORI

Give her the air. [to Mosca] What can you say?

MOSCA

Give her the air. [to Mosca] What can you say? My wound,
136May it please your wisdoms, speaks for me, received
137In aid of my good patron, when he missed
138His sought-for father, when that well-taught dame
139Had her cue given her, to cry out, “a rape!”

BONARIO

140O, most laid impudence! Fathers—

3 AVOCATORI

O, most laid impudence! Fathers— Sir, be silent;
141You had your hearing free, so must they theirs.

2 AVOCATORI

142I do begin to doubt the imposture here.

4 AVOCATORI

143This woman has too many moods.

VOLTORE

This woman has too many moods. Grave fathers,
144She is a creature of a most professed
145And prostituted lewdness.

CORVINO

And prostituted lewdness. Most impetuous,
146Unsatisfied, grave fathers!

VOLTORE

Unsatisfied, grave fathers! May her feignings
147Not take your wisdoms, but this day she baited
148A stranger, a grave knight, with her loose eyes,
149And more lascivious kisses. This man saw them
150Together on the water, in a gondola.

MOSCA

151Here is the lady herself, that saw them too;
152Without; who then had in the open streets
153Pursued them, but for saving her knight's honor.

1 AVOCATORI

154Produce that lady.

2 AVOCATORI

Produce that lady. Let her come.

[Exit Mosca.]

4 AVOCATORI

Produce that lady. Let her come. These things,
155They strike with wonder!

3 AVOCATORI

They strike with wonder! I am turned a stone!

ACT 4, SCENE 6

(Enter Mosca and Lady Would-Be.)

MOSCA.

1Be resolute, madam.

LADY WOULD-BE

Be resolute, madam. Aye, this same is she.
2Out, thou chameleon harlot! Now thine eyes
3Vie tears with the hyena. Dar'st thou look
4Upon my wronged face?– I cry your pardons.
5I fear I have forgettingly transgressed
6Against the dignity of the court –

2 AVOCATORI

Against the dignity of the court – No, madam.

LADY WOULD-BE

7And been exorbitant –

2 AVOCATORI

And been exorbitant – You have not, lady.

4 AVOCATORI

8These proofs are strong.

LADY WOULD-BE

These proofs are strong. Surely, I had no purpose
9To scandalize your honours, or my sex's.

3 AVOCATORI

10We do believe it.

LADY WOULD-BE

We do believe it. Surely, you may believe it.

2 AVOCATORI

11Madam, we do.

LADY WOULD-BE

Madam, we do. Indeed you may. My breeding
12Is not so coarse –

4 AVOCATORI

Is not so coarse – We know it.

LADY WOULD-BE

Is not so coarse – We know it. To offend
13With pertinacy –

3 AVOCATORI

With pertinacy – Lady –

LADY WOULD-BE

With pertinacy – Lady – Such a presence!
14No, surely.

1 AVOCATORI

No, surely. We well think it.

LADY WOULD-BE

No, surely. We well think it. You may think it.

1 AVOCATORI

15Let her o'ercome. What witnesses have you
16To make good your report?

BONARIO

To make good your report? Our consciences.

CELIA

17And heaven, that never fails the innocent.

4 AVOCATORI

18These are no testimonies.

BONARIO

These are no testimonies. Not in your courts,
19Where multitude and clamour overcomes.

1 AVOCATORI

20Nay, then you do wax insolent.

(Volpone is brought in, as impotent.)

VOLTORE

Nay, then you do wax insolent. Here, here,
21The testimony comes, that will convince,
22And put to utter dumbness their bold tongues:
23See here, grave fathers, here's the ravisher,
24The rider on men's wives, the great impostor,
25The grand voluptuary! Do you not think
26These limbs should affect venery? Or these eyes
27Covet a concubine? Pray you mark these hands;
28Are they not fit to stroke a lady's breasts?–
29Perhaps he doth dissemble!

BONARIO

Perhaps he doth dissemble! So he does.

VOLTORE

30Would you have him tortured?

BONARIO

Would you have him tortured? I would have him proved.

VOLTORE

31Best try him then with goads, or burning irons;
32Put him to the strappado: I have heard
33The rack hath cured the gout; faith, give it him,
34And help him of a malady; be courteous.
35I'll undertake, before these honored fathers,
36He shall have yet as many left diseases
37As she has known adulterers, or thou strumpets.
38O, my most equal hearers, if these deeds,
39Acts of this bold and most exorbitant strain,
40May pass with sufferance, what one citizen
41But owes the forfeit of his life, yea, fame,
42To him that dares traduce him? Which of you
43Are safe, my honoured fathers? I would ask,
44With leave of your grave fatherhoods, if their plot
45Have any face or colour like to truth?
46Or if, unto the dullest nostril here,
47It smell not rank, and most abhorrèd slander?
48I crave your care of this good gentleman,
49Whose life is much endangered by their fable;
50And as for them, I will conclude with this,
51That vicious persons, when they are hot and fleshed
52In impious acts, their constancy abounds:
53Damned deeds are done with greatest confidence.

1 AVOCATORI

54Take them to custody, and sever them.

2 AVOCATORI

55'Tis pity two such prodigies should live.

1 AVOCATORI

56Let the old gentleman be returned with care.
57I'm sorry your credulity hath wronged him.

[Exeunt Officers with Volpone.]

4 AVOCATORI

58These are two creatures!

3 AVOCATORI

These are two creatures! I’ve an earthquake in me.

2 AVOCATORI

59Their shame, even in their cradles, fled their faces.

4 AVOCATORI

60You have done a worthy service to the state, sir,
61In their discovery.

1 AVOCATORI

In their discovery. You shall hear, ere night,
62What punishment the court decrees upon them.

VOLTORE

63We thank your fatherhoods.

[Exeunt Avocatori, Notario, Officers with Bonario and Celia.]

We thank your fatherhoods. How like you it?

MOSCA

We thank your fatherhoods. How like you it? Rare.
64I'd have your tongue, sir, tipped with gold for this;
65I'd have you be the heir to the whole city;
66The earth I'd have want men, ere you want living:
67They're bound to erect your statue in St. Mark's.
68Signior Corvino, I would have you go
69And show yourself, that you have conquered.

CORVINO

And show yourself, that you have conquered. Yes.

MOSCA

70It was much better that you should profess
71Yourself a cuckold thus, than that the other
72Should have been proved.

CORVINO

Should have been proved. Nay, I considered that:
73Now it is her fault.

MOSCA

Now it is her fault. Then it had been yours.

CORVINO

74True; I do doubt this advocate still.

MOSCA

True; I do doubt this advocate still. I'faith
75You need not; I dare ease you of that care.

CORVINO

76I trust thee, Mosca.

MOSCA

I trust thee, Mosca. As your own soul, sir.

[Exit CORVINO.]

CORBACCIO

I trust thee, Mosca. As your own soul, sir. Mosca!

MOSCA

77Now for your business, sir.

CORBACCIO

Now for your business, sir. How! Have you business?

MOSCA

78Yes, yours, sir.

CORBACCIO

Yes, yours, sir. O, none else?

MOSCA

Yes, yours, sir. O, none else? None else, not I.

CORBACCIO

79Be careful, then.

MOSCA

Be careful, then. Rest you with both your eyes, sir.

CORBACCIO

80Dispatch it.

MOSCA

Dispatch it. Instantly.

CORBACCIO

Dispatch it. Instantly. And look that all,
81Whatever, be put in, jewels, plate, moneys.
82Household stuff, bedding, curtains.

MOSCA

Household stuff, bedding, curtains. Curtain-rings, sir.
83Only the advocate's fee must be deducted.

CORBACCIO

84I'll pay him now; you'll be too prodigal.

MOSCA

85Sir, I must tender it.

CORBACCIO

Sir, I must tender it. Two cecchines is well?

MOSCA

86No, six, sir.

CORBACCIO

No, six, sir. 'Tis too much.

MOSCA

No, six, sir. 'Tis too much. He talked a great while;
87You must consider that, sir.

CORBACCIO

You must consider that, sir. Well, there's three –

MOSCA

88I'll give it him.

CORBACCIO

I'll give it him. Do so, and there's for thee.

[Exit Corbaccio.]

MOSCA

89Bountiful bones! What horrid strange offence
90Did he commit 'gainst nature, in his youth,
91Worthy this age? [To Voltore.] You see, sir, how I work
92Unto your ends: take you no notice.

VOLTORE

Unto your ends: take you no notice. No,
93I'll leave you.

[Exit Voltore.]

MOSCA

I'll leave you. All is yours, the devil and all:
94Good advocate— Madam, I'll bring you home.

LADY WOULD-BE

95No, I'll go see your patron.

MOSCA

No, I'll go see your patron. That you shall not:
96I'll tell you why. My purpose is to urge
97My patron to reform his will; and for
98The zeal you have shown to-day, whereas before
99You were but third or fourth, you shall be now
100Put in the first: which would appear as begged
101If you were present. Therefore –

LADY WOULD-BE

If you were present. Therefore – You shall sway me.

[Exeunt.]

ACT 5

SCENE 1

(Enter Volpone.)

VOLPONE

1Well, I am here, and all this brunt is past.
2I ne'er was in dislike with my disguise
3Till this fled moment: here 'twas good, in private;
4But in your public, – cavè whilst I breathe.
5'Fore God, my left leg 'gan to have the cramp,
6And I apprehended straight some power had struck me
7With a dead palsy: well, I must be merry,
8And shake it off. A many of these fears
9Would put me into some villainous disease,
10Should they come thick upon me: I'll prevent 'em.
11Give me a bowl of lusty wine, to fright
12This humour from my heart. (He drinks.) – Hum, hum, hum!
13'Tis almost gone already; I shall conquer.
14Any device, now, of rare ingenious knavery,
15That would possess me with a violent laughter,
16Would make me up again. (Drinks again.) So, so, so, so.
17This heat is life; 'tis blood by this time:– Mosca!

ACT 5, SCENE 2

[Enter MOSCA.]

MOSCA

1How now, sir? Does the day look clear again?
2Are we recovered, and wrought out of error,
3Into our way, to see our path before us?
4Is our trade free once more?

VOLPONE

Is our trade free once more? Exquisite, Mosca!

MOSCA

5Was it not carried learnedly?

VOLPONE

Was it not carried learnedly? And stoutly:
6Good wits are greatest in extremities.

MOSCA

7It were a folly beyond thought, to trust
8Any grand act unto a cowardly spirit:
9You are not taken with it enough, methinks.

VOLPONE

10O, more than if I had enjoyed the wench:
11The pleasure of all woman-kind's not like it.

MOSCA

12Why, now you speak, sir. We must here be fixed;
13Here we must rest; this is our master-piece;
14We cannot think to go beyond this.

VOLPONE

We cannot think to go beyond this. True,
15Thou hast played thy prize, my precious Mosca.

MOSCA

Thou hast played thy prize, my precious Mosca. Nay, sir,
16To gull the court –

VOLPONE

To gull the court – And quite divert the torrent
17Upon the innocent.

MOSCA

Upon the innocent. Yes, and to make
18So rare a music out of discords –

VOLPONE

So rare a music out of discords – Right.
19That yet to me's the strangest, how thou hast borne it!
20That these, being so divided 'mongst themselves,
21Should not scent somewhat, or in me or thee,
22Or doubt their own side.

MOSCA

Or doubt their own side. True, they will not see't.
23Too much light blinds them, I think. Each of them
24Is so possessed and stuffed with his own hopes,
25That any thing unto the contrary,
26Never so true, or never so apparent,
27Never so palpable, they will resist it –

VOLPONE

28Like a temptation of the devil.

MOSCA

Like a temptation of the devil. Right, sir.
29Merchants may talk of trade, and your great signiors
30Of land that yields well; but if Italy
31Have any glebe more fruitful than these fellows,
32I am deceived. Did not your advocate rare?

VOLPONE

33O – "My most honoured fathers, my grave fathers,
34Under correction of your fatherhoods,
35What face of truth is here? If these strange deeds
36May pass, most honored fathers" – I had much ado
37To forbear laughing.

MOSCA

To forbear laughing. It seemed to me, you sweat, sir.

VOLPONE

38In troth, I did a little.

MOSCA

In troth, I did a little. But confess, sir,
39Were you not daunted?

VOLPONE

Were you not daunted? In good faith, I was
40A little in a mist, but not dejected;
41Never, but still my self.

MOSCA

Never, but still my self. I think it, sir.
42Now, so truth help me, I must needs say this, sir,
43And out of conscience for your advocate:
44He’s taken pains, in faith, sir, and deserved,
45In my poor judgment, I speak it under favour,
46Not to contrary you, sir, very richly –
47Well – to be cozened.

VOLPONE

Well – to be cozened. Troth, and I think so too,
48By that I heard him, in the latter end.

MOSCA

49O, but before, sir: had you heard him first
50Draw it to certain heads, then aggravate,
51Then use his vehement figures – I looked still
52When he would shift a shirt: and, doing this
53Out of pure love, no hope of gain –

VOLPONE

Out of pure love, no hope of gain – 'Tis right.
54I cannot answer him, Mosca, as I would,
55Not yet; but for thy sake, at thy entreaty,
56I will begin, even now– to vex them all,
57This very instant.

MOSCA

This very instant. Good sir.

VOLPONE

This very instant. Good sir. Call the dwarf
58And eunuch forth.

MOSCA

And eunuch forth. Castrone, Nano!

[Enter Castrone and Nano.]

NANO

And eunuch forth. Castrone, Nano! Here.

VOLPONE

59Shall we have a jig now?

MOSCA

Shall we have a jig now? What you please, sir.

VOLPONE

60Go, straight give out about the streets, you two,
61That I am dead; do it with constancy,
62Sadly, do you hear? Impute it to the grief
63Of this late slander.

[Exeunt Castrone and Nano.]

MOSCA

Of this late slander. What do you mean, sir?

VOLPONE

Of this late slander. What do you mean, sir? Oh,
64I shall have instantly my Vulture, Crow,
65Raven, come flying hither, on the news,
66To peck for carrion, my she-wolf, and all,
67Greedy, and full of expectation –

MOSCA

68And then to have it ravished from their mouths?

VOLPONE

69'Tis true. I will have thee put on a gown,
70And take upon thee, as thou wert mine heir:
71Show them a will: open that chest, and reach
72Forth one of those that has the blanks; I'll straight
73Put in thy name.

MOSCA

Put in thy name. [Getting a blank will] It will be rare, sir.

VOLPONE

Put in thy name. [Getting a blank will] It will be rare, sir. Aye,
74When they ev’n gape, and find themselves deluded –

MOSCA

75Yes.

VOLPONE

Yes. And thou use them scurvily!
76Dispatch, get on thy gown.

MOSCA

Dispatch, get on thy gown. (Dressing.) But, what, sir, if they ask
77After the body?

VOLPONE

After the body? Say, it was corrupted.

MOSCA

78I'll say it stunk, sir; and was fain to have it
79Coffined up instantly, and sent away.

VOLPONE

80Any thing; what thou wilt. Hold, here's my will.
81Get thee a cap, a count-book, pen and ink,
82Papers afore thee; sit as thou wert taking
83An inventory of parcels. I'll get up
84Behind the curtain, on a stool, and hearken;
85Sometime peep over, see how they do look,
86With what degrees their blood doth leave their faces.
87O, 'twill afford me a rare meal of laughter!

MOSCA

88Your advocate will turn stark dull upon it.

VOLPONE

89It will take off his oratory's edge.

MOSCA

90But your clarissimo, old round-back, he
91Will crump you like a hog-louse, with the touch.

VOLPONE

92And what Corvino?

MOSCA

And what Corvino? O, sir, look for him,
93To-morrow morning, with a rope and dagger,
94To visit all the streets; he must run mad.
95My lady too, that came into the court,
96To bear false witness for your worship –

VOLPONE

To bear false witness for your worship – Yes,
97And kissed me 'fore the fathers, when my face
98Flowed all with oils.

MOSCA

Flowed all with oils. And sweat– sir. Why, your gold
99Is such another med’cine, it dries up
100All those offensive savors: it transforms
101The most deformed, and restores them lovely,
102As 'twere the strange poetical girdle. Jove
103Could not invent t'himself a shroud more subtle
104To pass Acrisius' guards. It is the thing
105Makes all the world her grace, her youth, her beauty.

VOLPONE

106I think she loves me.

MOSCA

I think she loves me. Who? The lady, sir?
107She's jealous of you.

VOLPONE

She's jealous of you. Dost thou say so?

[Knocking outside.]

MOSCA

She's jealous of you. Dost thou say so? Hark,
108There's some already.

VOLPONE

There's some already. Look.

MOSCA

There's some already. Look. It is the Vulture;
109He has the quickest scent.

VOLPONE

He has the quickest scent. I'll to my place,
110Thou to thy posture.

[Conceals himself.]

MOSCA

Thou to thy posture. I am set.

VOLPONE

Thou to thy posture. I am set. But, Mosca,
111Play the artificer now, torture them rarely.

ACT 5, SCENE 3

[Enter Voltore.]

VOLTORE

1How now, my Mosca?

MOSCA

How now, my Mosca? Turkey carpets, nine –

VOLTORE

2Taking an inventory! That is well.

MOSCA

3Two suits of bedding, tissue–

VOLTORE

Two suits of bedding, tissue– Where's the will?
4Let me read that the while.

[Enter Corbaccio in a sedan chair.]

CORBACCIO

Let me read that the while. So, set me down,
5And get you home.

[Exeunt servants.]

VOLTORE

And get you home. Is he come now, to trouble us!

MOSCA

6Of cloth of gold, two more –

CORBACCIO

Of cloth of gold, two more – Is it done, Mosca?

MOSCA

7Of several velvets, eight –

VOLTORE

Of several velvets, eight – I like his care.

CORBACCIO

8Dost thou not hear?

[Enter Corvino.]

CORBACCIO

Dost thou not hear? Ha! is the hour come, Mosca?

(Volpone peeps from behind a traverse.)

VOLTORE

9[aside] Aye, now they muster.aparte

CORVINO

[aside] Aye, now they muster. What does the advocate here,
10Or this Corbaccio?

CORBACCIO

Or this Corbaccio? What do these here?

[Enter Lady Politic Would-be.]

LADY WOULD-BE

Or this Corbaccio? What do these here? Mosca!
11Is his thread spun?

MOSCA

Is his thread spun? Eight chests of linen–

VOLPONE

Is his thread spun? Eight chests of linen– O,
12My fine dame Would-be, too!

CORVINO

My fine dame Would-be, too! Mosca, the will,
13That I may show it these, and rid them hence.

MOSCA

14Six chests of diaper, four of damask. – There.

[Gives Corvino the will.]

CORBACCIO

15Is that the will?

MOSCA

Is that the will? Down-beds and bolsters –

VOLPONE

Is that the will? Down-beds and bolsters – [Aside.] Rare!aparte
16Be busy still. Now they begin to flutter;
17They never think of me. Look, see, see, see!
18How their swift eyes run over the long deed
19Unto the name, and to the legacies,
20What is bequeathed them there –

MOSCA

What is bequeathed them there – Ten suits of hangings –

VOLPONE

21[Aside.] Aye, in their garters, Mosca. Now their hopesaparte
22Are at the gasp.

VOLTORE

Are at the gasp. Mosca the heir!
Are at the gasp. Mosca the heir! CORBACCIO What's that?

VOLPONE

23[Aside.] My advocate is dumb; look to my merchant,aparte
24He has heard of some strange storm, a ship is lost,
25He faints; my lady will swoon. Old glazen-eyes,
26He hath not reached his despair yet.

CORBACCIO

He hath not reached his despair yet. All these
27Are out of hope; I am, sure, the man.

CORVINO

Are out of hope; I am, sure, the man. But, Mosca –

MOSCA

28Two cabinets.

CORVINO

Two cabinets. Is this in earnest?

MOSCA

Two cabinets. Is this in earnest? One
29Of ebony –

CORVINO

Of ebony – Or do you but delude me?

MOSCA

30The other, mother-of-pearl –I am very busy.
31Good faith, it is a fortune thrown upon me –
32Item, one salt of agate — not my seeking.

LADY WOULD-BE

33Do you hear, sir?

MOSCA

Do you hear, sir? A perfumed box - Pray you forbear,
34You see I’m troubled – made of an onyx–

LADY WOULD-BE

You see I’m troubled – made of an onyx– How?

MOSCA

35Tomorrow or next day, I shall be at leisure
36To talk with you all.

CORVINO

To talk with you all. Is this my large hope's issue?

LADY WOULD-BE

37Sir, I must have a fairer answer.

MOSCA

Sir, I must have a fairer answer. Madam!
38Marry, and shall: pray you, fairly quit my house.
39Nay, raise no tempest with your looks; but hark you,
40Remember what your ladyship offered me
41To put you in an heir; go to, think on it:
42And what you said e'en your best madams did
43For maintenance; and why not you? Enough.
44Go home, and use the poor Sir Pol, your knight, well,
45For fear I tell some riddles; go, be melancholy.

[Exit Lady Politic Would-be]

VOLPONE

46O, my fine devil!

CORVINO

O, my fine devil! Mosca, pray you a word.

MOSCA

47Lord! Will you not take your dispatch hence yet?
48Methinks, of all, you should have been the example.
49Why should you stay here? With what thought, what promise?
50Hear you; do you not know, I know you an ass,
51And that you would most fain have been a wittol,
52If fortune would have let you? That you are
53A declared cuckold, on good terms? This pearl,
54You'll say, was yours? Right. This diamond?
55I'll not deny't, but thank you. Much here else?
56It may be so. Why, think that these good works
57May help to hide your bad. I'll not betray you;
58Although you be but extraordinary
59And have it only in title, it sufficeth.
60Go home, be melancholic too, or mad.

[Exit Corvino.]

VOLPONE

61[Aside.] Rare, Mosca! How his villainy becomes him!aparte

VOLTORE

62Certain he doth delude all these for me.

CORBACCIO

63Mosca the heir!

VOLPONE

Mosca the heir! [Aside.] O, his four eyes have found it.aparte

CORBACCIO

64I’m cozened, cheated, by a parasite slave;
65Harlot, thou hast gulled me.

MOSCA

Harlot, thou hast gulled me. Yes, sir. Stop your mouth,
66Or I shall draw the only tooth is left.
67Are not you he, that filthy covetous wretch,
68With the three legs, that here, in hope of prey,
69Have, any time this three years, snuffed about,
70With your most grovelling nose, and would have hired
71Me to the poisoning of my patron, sir?
72Are not you he that have to-day in court
73Professed the disinheriting of your son?
74Perjured yourself? Go home, and die, and stink.
75If you but croak a syllable, all comes out:
76Away, and call your porters. Go, go stink.

[Exit Corbaccio.]

VOLPONE

77[Aside.] Excellent varlet!aparte

VOLTORE

[Aside.] Excellent varlet! Now, my faithful Mosca,aparte
78I find thy constancy.

MOSCA

79Sir?

VOLTORE

Sir? Sincere.

MOSCA

Sir? Sincere. A table
80Of porphyry – I mar’l you'll be thus troublesome.

VOLTORE

81Nay, leave off now, they are gone.

MOSCA

Nay, leave off now, they are gone. Why, who are you?
82What? Who did send for you? O, cry you mercy,
83Reverend sir! Good faith, I am grieved for you,
84That any chance of mine should thus defeat
85Your (I must needs say) most deserving travails:
86But I protest, sir, it was cast upon me,
87And I could almost wish to be without it,
88But that the will of the dead must be observed.
89Marry, my joy is that you need it not;
90You have a gift, sir (thank your education),
91Will never let you want, while there are men,
92And malice, to breed causes. Would I had
93But half the like, for all my fortune, sir!
94If I have any suits, as I do hope;
95Things being so easy and direct, I shall not,
96I will make bold with your obstreperous aid,
97Conceive me, –for your fee, sir. In mean time
98You that have so much law, I know have the conscience
99Not to be covetous of what is mine.
100Good sir, I thank you for my plate; 'twill help
101To set up a young man. Good faith; you look
102As you were costive; best go home and purge, sir.

[Exit Voltore.]

VOLPONE

103[coming forward] Bid him eat lettuce well. My witty mischief,
104Let me embrace thee. O, that I could now
105Transform thee to a Venus! –Mosca, go,
106Straight take my habit of clarissimo,
107And walk the streets; be seen, torment them more:
108We must pursue, as well as plot. Who would
109Have lost this feast?

MOSCA

Have lost this feast? I doubt it will lose them.

VOLPONE

110O, my recovery shall recover all.
111That I could now but think on some disguise
112To meet them in, and ask them questions:
113How I would vex them still at every turn!

MOSCA

114Sir, I can fit you.

VOLPONE

Sir, I can fit you. Canst thou?

MOSCA

Sir, I can fit you. Canst thou? Yes, I know
115One o' the Commendadori, sir, so like you;
116Him will I straight make drunk, and bring you his habit.

VOLPONE

117A rare disguise, and answering thy brain!
118O, I will be a sharp disease unto them.

MOSCA

119Sir, you must look for curses –

VOLPONE

Sir, you must look for curses – Till they burst!
120The Fox fares ever best when he is curst.

[Exeunt.]

ACT 5, SCENE 4

[Enter Peregrine in disguise, and three Merchants.]

PEREGRINE

1Am I enough disguised?

FIRST MERCHANT

Am I enough disguised? I warrant you.

PEREGRINE

2All my ambition is to fright him only.

SECOND MERCHANT

3If you could ship him away, 'twere excellent.

THIRD MERCHANT

4To Zant, or to Aleppo?

PEREGRINE

To Zant, or to Aleppo? Yes, and have his
5Adventures put i'th’ Book of voyages,
6And his gulled story registered for truth.
7Well, gentlemen, when I am in a while,
8And that you think us warm in our discourse,
9Know your approaches.

FIRST MERCHANT

Know your approaches. Trust it to our care.

[Exeunt Merchants, enter Waiting-woman.]

PEREGRINE

10Save you, fair lady. Is sir Pol within?

WOMAN

11I do not know, sir.

PEREGRINE

I do not know, sir. Pray you say unto him,
12Here is a merchant, upon earnest business,
13Desires to speak with him.

WOMAN

Desires to speak with him. I will see, sir.

PEREGRINE

Desires to speak with him. I will see, sir. Pray you.
14[Aside.] I see the family is all female here.aparte

WOMAN

15He says, sir, he has weighty affairs of state
16That now require him whole; some other time
17You may possess him.

PEREGRINE

You may possess him. Pray you say again,
18If those require him whole, these will exact him,
19Whereof I bring him tidings.

[Exit Woman.]

Whereof I bring him tidings. What might be
20His grave affair of state, now! How to make
21Bolognian sausages here in Venice, sparing
22One o' the ingredients?

[Re-Enter Woman.]

WOMAN

One o' the ingredients? Sir, he says, he knows
23By your word “tidings” that you are no statesman,
24And therefore wills you stay.

PEREGRINE

And therefore wills you stay. Sweet, pray you return him;
25I have not read so many proclamations,
26And studied them for words, as he has done–
27But – here he deigns to come.

[Enter Sir Politic.]

SIR POLITIC

But – here he deigns to come. Sir, I must crave
28Your courteous pardon. There hath chanced to-day
29Unkind disaster 'twixt my lady and me;
30And I was penning my apology,
31To give her satisfaction, as you came now.

PEREGRINE

32Sir, I am grieved I bring you worse disaster:
33The gentleman you met at the port to-day,
34That told you, he was newly arrived –

SIR POLITIC

That told you, he was newly arrived – Aye, was
35A fugitive punk?

PEREGRINE

A fugitive punk? No, sir, a spy set on you;
36And he has made relation to the Senate,
37That you professed to him to have a plot
38To sell the state of Venice to the Turk.

SIR POLITIC

39O me!

PEREGRINE

O me! For which, warrants are signed by this time,
40To apprehend you, and to search your study
41For papers –

SIR POLITIC

For papers – Alas, sir, I have none, but notes
42Drawn out of play-books –

PEREGRINE

Drawn out of play-books – All the better, sir.

SIR POLITIC

43And some essays. What shall I do?

PEREGRINE

And some essays. What shall I do? Sir, best
44Convey yourself into a sugar-chest;
45Or, if you could lie round, a frail were rare,
46And I could send you aboard.

SIR POLITIC

And I could send you aboard. Sir, I but talked so,
47For discourse sake merely.

(They knock without.)

PEREGRINE

For discourse sake merely. Hark! they are there.

SIR POLITIC

48I am a wretch, a wretch!

PEREGRINE

I am a wretch, a wretch! What will you do, sir?
49Have you ne'er a currant-butt to leap into?
50They'll put you to the rack; you must be sudden.

SIR POLITIC

51Sir, I have an engine –

THIRD MERCHANT

Sir, I have an engine – Sir Politic Would-be!

SECOND MERCHANT

52Where is he?

SIR POLITIC

Where is he? That I have thought upon before time.

PEREGRINE

53What is it?

SIR POLITIC

What is it? I shall ne'er endure the torture.
54Marry, it is, sir, of a tortoise-shell,
55Fitted for these extremities. Pray you, sir, help me.
56[Get into the shell.] Here I’ve a place, sir, to put back my legs,
57Please you to lay it on, sir. With this cap,
58And my black gloves. I'll lie sir, like a tortoise,
59Till they are gone.

PEREGRINE

Till they are gone. And call you this an engine?

SIR POLITIC

60Mine own device – Good sir, bid my wife's women
61To burn my papers.

[Exit Peregrine and Woman. The three Merchants rush in.]

FIRST MERCHANT

To burn my papers. Where is he hid?

THIRD MERCHANT

To burn my papers. Where is he hid? We must,
62And will sure find him.

SECOND MERCHANT

And will sure find him. Which is his study?

[Re-enter Peregrine.]

FIRST MERCHANT

And will sure find him. Which is his study? What
63Are you, sir?

PEREGRINE

Are you, sir? I am a merchant, that came here
64To look upon this tortoise.

THIRD MERCHANT

To look upon this tortoise. How!

FIRST MERCHANT

To look upon this tortoise. How! St. Mark!
65What beast is this!

PEREGRINE

What beast is this! It is a fish.

SECOND MERCHANT

What beast is this! It is a fish. Come out here!

PEREGRINE

66Nay, you may strike him, sir, and tread upon him;
67He'll bear a cart.

FIRST MERCHANT

He'll bear a cart. What, to run over him?

PEREGRINE

He'll bear a cart. What, to run over him? Yes.

THIRD MERCHANT

68Let's jump upon him.

SECOND MERCHANT

Let's jump upon him. Can he not go?

PEREGRINE

Let's jump upon him. Can he not go? He creeps, sir.

FIRST MERCHANT

69Let's see him creep.

PEREGRINE

Let's see him creep. No, good sir, you will hurt him.

SECOND MERCHANT

70Heart, I will see him creep, or prick his guts.

THIRD MERCHANT

71Come out here!

PEREGRINE

Come out here! Pray you, sir!
72(To Sir Politic.) Creep a little.

FIRST MERCHANT

(To Sir Politic.) Creep a little. Forth.

SECOND MERCHANT

73Yet farther.

PEREGRINE

Yet farther. Good sir! - Creep.

SECOND MERCHANT

Yet farther. Good sir! - Creep. We'll see his legs.

[They pull off the shell and discover him.]

THIRD MERCHANT

74Godso, he has garters!

FIRST MERCHANT

Godso, he has garters! Aye, and gloves!

SECOND MERCHANT

Godso, he has garters! Aye, and gloves! Is this
75Your fearful tortoise?

PEREGRINE

Your fearful tortoise? Now, Sir Pol, we are even;
76For your next project I shall be prepared:
77I am sorry for the funeral of your notes, sir.

FIRST MERCHANT

78'Twere a rare motion to be seen in Fleet-Street.

SECOND MERCHANT

79Aye, in the Term.

FIRST MERCHANT

Aye, in the Term. Or Smithfield, in the fair.

THIRD MERCHANT

80Methinks 'tis but a melancholic sight.

PEREGRINE

81Farewell, most politic tortoise!

[Exeunt Peregrine and Merchants. Re-enter Waiting-woman.]

SIR POLITIC

Farewell, most politic tortoise! Where's my lady?
82Knows she of this?

WOMAN

Knows she of this? I know not, sir.

SIR POLITIC

Knows she of this? I know not, sir. Enquire.—

[Exit Woman.]

83O, I shall be the fable of all feasts,
84The freight of the gazetti, ship-boys’ tale;
85And, which is worst, even talk for ordinaries.

WOMAN

86My lady's come most melancholic home,
87And says, sir, she will straight to sea, for physic.

SIR POLITIC

88And I to shun this place and clime for ever,
89Creeping with house on back, and think it well
90To shrink my poor head in my politic shell.

[Exeunt.]

ACT 5, SCENE 5

[Enter Volpone, Mosca; the first, in the habit of a commendatore, and the other, of a clarissimo.]

VOLPONE

1Am I then like him?

MOSCA

Am I then like him? O, sir, you are he:
2No man can sever you.

VOLPONE

No man can sever you. Good.

MOSCA

No man can sever you. Good. But what am I?

VOLPONE

3'Fore heaven, a brave clarissimo; thou becom'st it!
4Pity thou wert not born one.

MOSCA

Pity thou wert not born one. If I hold
5My made one, 'twill be well.

VOLPONE

My made one, 'twill be well. I'll go and see
6What news first at the court.

[Exit]

MOSCA

What news first at the court. Do so. My Fox
7Is out of his hole, and ere he shall re-enter,
8I'll make him languish in his borrowed case,
9Except he come to composition with me.
10Androgyno, Castrone, Nano!

[Enter Androgyno, Castrone, and Nano.]

ALL

Androgyno, Castrone, Nano! Here.

MOSCA

11Go, recreate yourselves abroad; go sport.

[Exeunt Androgyno, Castrone, and Nano.]

12So, now I have the keys, and am possessed.
13Since he will needs be dead afore his time,
14I'll bury him or gain by him: I am his heir,
15And so will keep me, till he share at least.
16To cozen him of all, were but a cheat
17Well placed; no man would construe it a sin:
18Let his sport pay for't. This is called the Fox-Trap.

[Exit.]

ACT 5, SCENE 6

[Enter Corbaccio and Corvino.]

CORBACCIO

1They say, the court is set.

CORVINO

They say, the court is set. We must maintain
2Our first tale good, for both our reputations.

CORBACCIO

3Why, mine's no tale: my son would there have killed me.

CORVINO

4That's true, I had forgot. Mine is, I'm sure.
5But for your will, sir.

CORBACCIO

But for your will, sir. Aye, I'll come upon him
6For that hereafter, now his patron's dead.

[Enter Volpone.]

VOLPONE

7Signior Corvino! And Corbaccio! sir,
8Much joy unto you.

CORVINO

Much joy unto you. Of what?

VOLPONE

ENTRENT VOLPONE ET MOSCA.

VOLPONE:

Bonjour. Et maintenant occupons-nous de notre or. Ouvre l’autel que je puisse voir mon saint! (Mosca tire un rideau. On voit des piles d’or, de vaisselles d’argent, des joyaux, etc.). Salut, mon âme et celle du monde! Je suis plus heureux que la terre féconde voyant le soleil attendu paraître entre les cornes du Bélier céleste, quand j’examine ta splendeur qui éteint la sienne. Reposant là, parmi tant d’autres richesses, tu sembles une flamme dans la nuit, un jour se faisant un chemin dans le chaos tandis que l’obscurité se réfugie au centre du monde. O toi, fils du soleil, dieu plus étincelant que ton père, laisse-moi t’embrasser, t’adorer ainsi que toutes les reliques du trésor sacré enfermé dans cette chambre bénie! Comme les poètes ont eu raison de donner ton nom glorieux à l’âge où ils auraient voulu vivre! N’es-tu pas la meilleure des choses, prodiguant plus de joie que les enfants, les parents, les amis, que tous les rêves éveillés que l’on fait sur terre? Ton éclat, réfléchi dans les yeux de Vénus aurait dû lui faire enfanter vingt mille Cupidons! Telles sont les beautés et tel est noire amour! O richesse, sainte muette qui fait parler tous les hommes, tu n’agis pas par toi-même, mais tu permets de tout accomplir. Tu es le prix des âmes; l’enfer lui-même, embelli par toi, devient plus enviable que le ciel! Tu représentes la vertu, la renommée, l’honneur, tout! Qui peut t’obtenir sera noble, vaillant, honnête, sage...

MOSCA:

Et tout ce qu’il voudra, monsieur. La richesse est dans cette vie un plus grand bien que la sagesse.

VOLPONE:

Voilà une vérité, mon cher Mosca. Et pourtant je suis plus fier des procédés par moi employés pour acquérir la richesse que de sa possession, car je ne l’ai pas gagnée comme tout le monde. Je ne fais pas de commerce, ne me fie pas au hasard, ne blesse pas la terre avec des charrues. Je n’engraisse pas des bestiaux pour achalander les boucheries; je ne forge pas le fer, n’ai pas de moulins pour moudre l’huile ou le blé, d’hommes pour les broyer; je ne souffle pas le verre délicat, je n’expose pas des navires à la fureur des mers qu’ils sillonnent; je ne spécule pas dans les banques, et je ne pratique pas l’usure.

MOSCA:

Non, monsieur, vous ne dévorez pas les prodigues. Il y en a qui avalent un héritier confiant, comme un Hollandais ses pilules de beurre, sans être payés pour cela; qui arrachent de leurs lits de pauvres pères de famille pour les ensevelir vivants dans quelque prison verrouillée d’où leurs os ne sortiront que lorsque la chair sera pourrie. Votre nature bienveillante abhorre de semblables moyens. Vous n’aimez pas voir des larmes de veuves on d’orphelins arroser votre seuil, entendre sous votre toit leurs cris pitoyables ébranler l’air.

VOLPONE:

Tu as raison, Mosca. Je déteste cela.

MOSCA:

Vous ne ressemblez pas au batteur en grange qui, avec un terrible fléau, surveille son blé et, mourant de faim, n’osant pas en dérober un grain, préfère se nourrir de mauves et d’herbes amères; ni au marchand qui, après avoir rempli ses celliers de généreux vins provenant de la Romagne ou de Candie, boit la lie des vinaigres lombards. Vous dédaignez de coucher sur la paille, tandis que les mites et les vers se nourriraient de vos somptueuses tentures et de vos lits moelleux. Vous savez user de vos richesses, et en distribuer une partie à votre pauvre intendant, à votre nain, à votre hermaphrodite, a votre eunuque, à tous ceux qui vous entourent et que votre bon plaisir entretient.

VOLPONE:

Lui donnant de l’argent. Voilà pour toi, Mosca. Prends-le de ma main. Tout ce que tu dis est vrai et ce sont les envieux qui t’appellent parasite. Va me chercher mon nain, mon eunuque, mon fou, afin qu’ils me divertissent. (Sort Mosca). Que puis-je faire, sinon choyer mon génie et profiter librement de tous les avantages que peut me procurer la fortune? Je n’ai ni femme, ni parent, ni enfant, ni alliés à constituer comme héritiers. Héritera qui je choisirai. C’est pourquoi les gens ont l’œil sur moi, pourquoi de nouveaux visiteurs affluent journellement dans ma maison, hommes et femmes de tout âge, m’apportant des présents, m’envoyant de la vaisselle d’argent, de l’argent monnayé, des bijoux, dans l’espérance, lorsque je mourrai, (ce qu’ils attendent impatiemment), que je leur retourne dix fois plus qu’ils ne m’auront donné. D’autres, plus intéressés encore, cherchent à m’accaparer et luttent entre eux à qui me comblera le plus de cadeaux et me donnera le plus de preuves d’affection. Je les laisse faire, m’amusant de leurs espérances, en tirant tout le profit possible, entretenant leurs tendresses. Je les tiens tous dans la main, laissant la cerise effleurer leurs lèvres, pour la leur retirer aussitôt de la bouche. Eh bien?

(Rentre MOSCA avec NANO, ANDROGYNO et CASTRONE).

NANO:

Maintenant, place pour ces nouveaux joueurs. Ils ne vous apportent ni pièce de théâtre, ni représentation comme on en donne dans les Universités. Ils vous supplient donc, quel que soit le récit, de ne point trop éplucher la cadence de leurs vers. Si cela vous étonne, vous serez plus étonné encore d’apprendre que dans le corps d’Androgyno est enfermée l’âme de Pythagore, ce jongleur devin, comme vous le verrez par la suite, laquelle âme vint d’abord d’Apollon, puis fut insufflée dans Aethalides, fils de Mercure, où elle acquit la faculté de rappeler tout ce qui avait été fait. Elle quitta Aethalides et alla aussitôt se loger chez Euphorbus aux cheveux d’or, qui fut tué de belle façon au siège de la vieille Troie par le cocu de Sparte. Elle se réfugia ensuite (je trouve cela dans ma charte) chez Hermotinus. A peine y était-elle qu’elle demanda asile à un Pyrrhus de Délos qui lui apprit à pécher. De là nous la retrouvons chez le sophiste de Grèce. Abandonnant Pythagore en faveur d’un joli morceau, Aspasie la courtisane, elle passa dans le corps d’une autre catin, pour s’agiter dans un philosophe, Cratès le cynique, comme elle le raconte. Depuis, des rois, des chevaliers, des mendiants, des esclaves, des lords, des fous l’ont enfermée; puis des bœufs, des ânes, des chameaux, des mules, des boucs, des blaireaux, où elle s’est complue à parler comme le coq du savetier. Mais je no suis pas venu pour discourir sur cette matière, sur son un, deux, trois, son grand serment par quatre, sa musique, son trigone, sa cuisse d’or, son discours sur la rotation des éléments, mais pour te demander comment tu as supporté ta dernière transformation et si tu as changé de vêtement dans ces jours de réformation?

ANDROGYNO:

Je me suis habillé en réformé, autant dire en fou, ainsi que vous le voyez, considérant toutes les vieilles doctrines comme des hérésies.

NANO:

N’as-tu jamais risqué des mets défendus par ton maître?

ANDROGYNO:

J'ai d’abord mangé du poisson quand je suis entré chez les Chartreux.

NANO:

Pourquoi alors as-tu renoncé à ton silence dogmatique?

ANDROGYNO:

Un avocat turbulent l’a voulu.

NANO:

O changement qui stupéfie! Quand le sieur avocat t’at-il chassé? Pour l’amour de Pythagore, quel corps as-tu alors habité?

ANDROGYNO:

Celui d’une bonne mule.

NANO:

De la façon tu pouvais manger des fèves?

ANDROGYNO:

Oui.

NANO:

De la mule, où as-tu passé?

ANDROGYNO:

Dans une bête tout à fait étrange, quelques écrivains l’appellent un âne; d'autres un frère précis, pur, illuminé, de ceux qui mangent de la viande et quelquefois se dévorent entre eux; de ceux qui publient des libelles, colportent des mensonges sanctifiés entre chaque cuillerée de pâté de la Nativité.

NANO:

Maintenant, par le ciel, assez de cette notion profane et parlons de la transmigration qui suivit.

ANDROGYNO:

J’habitai le corps où je suis encore.

NANO:

Un corps de délices, valant mieux que celui d’antan, le corps d’un hermaphrodite! Maintenant, dis-moi, chère âme, parmi tous ces changements quel corps choisirais-tu s’il fallait t’y fixer?

ANDROGYNO:

Celui que j’habite. Je vaudrais même n’en plus changer.

NANO:

Parce que tu peux jouir à la fois du plaisir de chaque sexe.

ANDROGYNO:

Hélas! Ces plaisirs sont vieillis et abandonnés! Je me félicite d'être l’âme d’un fou, la seule créature que je puisse qualifier de bénie, car les autres formes ne m’ont pas porté bonheur.

NANO:

Parle franchement, comme si tu habitais toujours le corps de Pythagore. Nous célébrerons cette savante opinion, camarade eunuque, comme il nous convient, avec tout notre esprit et tout notre talent, pour dignifier des membres spéciaux de la fraternité.

VOLPONE:

Hé bien! hé bien! Mosca, cela est-il de ton invention?

MOSCA:

Oui, s’il plaît à mon patron.

VOLPONE:

Cela me plaît, mon bon Mosca.

MOSCA:

En ce cas, j’en suis bien l’auteur.

NANO ET CASTRONE:

1chantant. Les fous sont la seule nation
2Digne de l’envie et de l’admiration des hommes.
3Libres de tout souci, de tout chagrin,
4Ils sont heureux et rendent heureux les autres.
5Tout ce qu’ils disent est d’or.
